subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: A force is a push or a pull, and once you can name the forces acting on something you can explain why it moves, why it stops, and why it stays exactly where it is. This unit names the forces you meet every day, shows that several always act at once, teaches you to draw them as arrows, and then looks at the one force that works without anything touching at all.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, experiments and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge
unit.reviewStatus: Authored from the Cambridge books — curriculum review required

objectives.text: Identify a range of forces (limited to gravity, applied forces, normal forces, upthrust, friction, air resistance and water resistance).
Know that an object may have multiple forces acting upon it, even when at rest.
Use force diagrams to show the name and direction of forces acting on an object.
Know the difference between a magnet and a magnetic material.
Know that forces act over a distance between magnets, and between a magnet and a magnetic material.
Know that magnets can have different magnetic strengths.

sourceDocuments: Cambridge Primary Science Teacher's Resource 5, topics on forces and magnetism

outcomes: Name the forces acting in an everyday situation.
Explain the difference between a push, a pull, and a force acting at a distance.
Recognise that an object at rest still has forces acting on it.
Draw a force diagram with arrows showing the name and direction of each force.
Tell a magnet apart from a magnetic material, and test which is which.
Describe how magnets attract and repel across a gap.
Compare the strength of two magnets fairly.

concepts.title: What a Force Does
concepts.explanation:
A FORCE is a push or a pull. That is the whole definition, and everything else in this unit is built on it. A force is measured in NEWTONS, written N, using a forcemeter - a spring that stretches further the harder it is pulled.

A force can do three things to an object, and only these three. It can make a still object start moving. It can change how a moving object moves - speeding it up, slowing it down, or turning it. And it can change an object's shape, which is what happens when you squeeze a ripe mango or stretch a rubber band.

Some forces need two things to be touching. An APPLIED FORCE is the push or pull you give something with your hand, a rope or an engine. FRICTION acts between two surfaces sliding past each other and always opposes the sliding, which is why a ball rolling on grass stops sooner than one on smooth concrete. AIR RESISTANCE and WATER RESISTANCE are friction with air and with water, and both grow the faster you move - which is why running feels harder into a wind and why swimming is slow work. A NORMAL FORCE is the push a surface gives back: the floor pushing up on your feet right now, which is the only reason you are not sinking through it. UPTHRUST is the upward push water gives anything placed in it, and it is why a bucket of water feels lighter under the surface than lifted out.

And one force needs no contact at all. GRAVITY pulls everything towards the centre of the Earth without touching it, which is why a dropped mango falls and why you have a weight at all.
concepts.example: A boy pulls a loaded cart along a dirt track. His hands give an applied force forward. Friction between the wheels and the track pushes backward. Gravity pulls the cart down, and the track pushes up on the wheels with a normal force. Four forces, on one cart, at one moment - and he can only feel one of them.

concepts.title: More Than One Force at Once
concepts.explanation:
Almost nothing ever has just one force on it. A book on a table, a boat on a lake, you on your chair - every one has at least two, and the interesting part is what happens when they are equal.

Take the book. Gravity pulls it down with, say, 4 N. The table pushes up on it with a normal force of 4 N. The two are the same size and point in opposite directions, so they CANCEL, and the book does not move. That is the important idea and it is easy to get backwards: the book is still NOT because no forces act on it, but because the forces that act on it balance.

The test is worth remembering. If you can think of a reason the object would fall, sink or slide, then there must be a second force stopping it. The book would fall, so something is holding it up. A boat would sink, so upthrust must be pushing it up as hard as gravity pulls it down. A parked lorry on a hill would roll, so friction must be holding it.

When the forces do not balance, motion changes. Add your hand to the book with a 2 N push sideways and nothing now cancels that push, so the book slides. Take the table away and the normal force goes with it, leaving gravity unopposed, and the book falls.

So 'balanced' does not mean 'still' and 'unbalanced' does not mean 'moving'. Balanced means the motion is not changing, which covers both a book sitting still and a canoe drifting at a steady speed.
concepts.example: Put a mango in a bowl of water and it floats, sitting lower in the water than you expected. Gravity is pulling it down and upthrust is pushing it up, and it sinks until the two are equal - then stops. Press it under with a finger and you have added a third force, and it moves again until you let go.

concepts.title: Drawing Forces as Arrows
concepts.explanation:
A force is invisible, and naming three or four of them in a sentence gets confusing quickly. Scientists draw them instead, and the drawing is called a FORCE DIAGRAM.

The rules are few. Draw the object simply - a box will do. For each force, draw an ARROW starting on the object and pointing the way the force acts. Label each arrow with the force's name. And if you know the sizes, make the arrows' lengths match them: a 10 N force gets an arrow twice as long as a 5 N one.

So the book on the table gets two arrows: one pointing down labelled gravity, one pointing up labelled normal force, both the same length because they are equal. The cart being pulled gets four. A falling stone gets one long arrow down for gravity and a short one up for air resistance.

The diagram earns its keep the moment you look at it, because balance becomes something you can SEE. Equal arrows in opposite directions mean nothing about the motion is changing. An arrow with nothing opposing it means the object will start moving that way. Two arrows the same way means a bigger effect than either alone.

One mistake is worth naming. Draw only the forces acting ON the object, not the forces it exerts on other things. The book pushes down on the table just as hard as the table pushes up on the book - but that push belongs on a diagram of the table, not of the book.
concepts.example: A diagram of a swimmer moving forward has four arrows: a long one forward labelled 'push from arms and legs', a shorter one backward labelled 'water resistance', one down labelled 'gravity' and one up labelled 'upthrust'. The forward arrow is the longest, so she is speeding up; the up and down arrows match, so she neither rises nor sinks.

concepts.title: Magnets and Magnetic Materials
concepts.explanation:
A MAGNET is an object that attracts certain metals towards it. A MAGNETIC MATERIAL is a material a magnet attracts. Those sound like the same thing and they are not, and the difference is the most-missed idea in this whole unit.

Hold a magnet near a steel nail and the nail jumps to it. The magnet is a magnet; the nail is a magnetic material. Now hold the nail near a second nail and nothing happens at all, because a magnetic material does not attract other things - it is only attracted BY a magnet. Every magnet is made of a magnetic material, and almost no magnetic material is a magnet.

Only a few materials are magnetic: iron, steel (which is mostly iron), nickel and cobalt. That is a short list, and everything else on Earth is not magnetic. This is the second common mistake - assuming all metals are magnetic. They are not: aluminium, copper, gold, silver and brass are all metals and a magnet ignores every one of them. A magnet is exactly how a recycling plant separates steel cans from aluminium ones.

And nothing that is not a metal is magnetic. Not wood, not plastic, not glass, not water, not paper. If a magnet picks something up, there is iron, steel, nickel or cobalt in it somewhere.

Every magnet has two ends called POLES, a north and a south, and they behave differently - which is the next concept.
concepts.example: A learner tests ten objects with a magnet: a steel spoon, an aluminium can, a copper wire, a plastic ruler, a glass marble, a coin, a nail, a wooden pencil, a rubber band and a paper clip. Only the spoon, the nail and the paper clip are attracted. All three are steel - and the aluminium can, which is certainly a metal, is not attracted at all.

concepts.title: Pulling Without Touching
concepts.explanation:
Every other force you can push with has to touch what it pushes. A magnet does not, and that is what makes it worth a unit of its own.

Bring a magnet slowly towards a paper clip on a table. Nothing happens, nothing happens - and then, while there is still a clear gap, the clip slides across and sticks. The force reached across the gap. It works through things too: a magnet will pick up a paper clip through a sheet of paper, a page of a book, a plastic ruler or a thin wooden board, because those materials do not block it.

The force gets STRONGER the closer the two are and weaker as they separate, which is why the clip lay still until the magnet was close. There is no sharp edge to it; it simply fades with distance.

And because a magnet has two poles, the force can go either way. Bring two NORTH poles together and they push apart - they REPEL. Two souths do the same. But bring a north near a south and they pull together - they ATTRACT. The rule is short: like poles repel, unlike poles attract. That is the only force in this unit that can push as well as pull without touching.

Repulsion is the better test of whether something is a magnet. A magnet attracts a magnetic material and it also attracts the other pole of another magnet - so attraction alone does not tell you which you are holding. Only another magnet will push back.
concepts.example: Float a bar magnet on a cork in a bowl of water and bring another magnet slowly towards one end. Turn the second magnet round and the floating one is pushed away instead of pulled in - it drifts off across the bowl. Nothing touched it either time.

concepts.title: Some Magnets Are Stronger Than Others
concepts.explanation:
Magnets are not all alike. A small button magnet off a fridge will hold one paper clip; a horseshoe magnet from the science cupboard will hold a chain of a dozen. MAGNETIC STRENGTH varies, and it can be measured rather than guessed.

There are two fair ways to compare two magnets. The first is to count how many paper clips each will hold in a hanging chain, clip to clip, until the chain breaks. The second, and the better one, is to find the greatest DISTANCE at which each will still start a clip moving: put a clip on a ruler, bring the magnet slowly along the ruler, and note the reading where the clip first twitches. A stronger magnet reaches further.

For either test to be fair, only the magnet may change. Use the same paper clips, the same surface, and the same way of measuring every time - and repeat each magnet several times, because where a clip first twitches is easy to misjudge by a few millimetres.

Strength is not the same as size. A small modern magnet made of special materials can easily beat a much larger old one. And a magnet can lose strength: dropping it hard, or heating it, jumbles the inside and weakens it, which is why magnets are stored in pairs with a small steel bar across the poles.
concepts.example: Two magnets are tested on the same ruler with the same clip. The fridge magnet starts the clip moving at 9 mm; the horseshoe magnet starts it at 41 mm. Each test is repeated three times and the readings agree within 2 mm, so the difference is real and the horseshoe magnet is far the stronger - even though the two are almost the same size.

explorations.title: Which Things Does a Magnet Pull?
explorations.context: To find out which materials are magnetic by testing them, rather than by guessing from what they look like.
explorations.prompt: Collect ten objects of different materials, including at least three metals that are not steel. Predict which will be attracted, then test each one with a magnet and record what actually happened.
explorations.answer: Only objects containing iron, steel, nickel or cobalt are attracted. Aluminium, copper and brass are metals and are NOT attracted, which is where most predictions go wrong.
explorations.hint: Sort your objects into two piles before you start - your predicted yes and your predicted no - and then test them. Comparing the two piles afterwards is where the surprise is.
explorations.explanation: Magnets and Magnetic Materials: only a few materials are magnetic, and being a metal is not enough. A magnet is exactly how a recycling plant tells a steel can from an aluminium one.

explorations.title: How Far Can a Magnet Reach?
explorations.context: To measure the distance across which a magnet can still act, and show that the force fades rather than stopping suddenly.
explorations.prompt: Lay a ruler flat with a paper clip at the zero mark. Slide a magnet slowly along the ruler towards it and read off the distance at which the clip first moves. Repeat three times and take the average.
explorations.answer: The clip moves while there is still a gap, and the distance is repeatable to within a few millimetres. A stronger magnet starts it moving from further away.
explorations.hint: Move the magnet very slowly near the end - a fast approach makes you overshoot the moment the clip first twitches.
explorations.explanation: Pulling Without Touching: the force reaches across a gap and grows stronger with closeness, which is why the clip lies still until the magnet is near.

explorations.title: What Is Holding It Up?
explorations.context: To show that an object sitting perfectly still has forces acting on it, by taking one of them away.
explorations.prompt: Rest a book on your flat palm and hold it steady. Describe what your hand can feel. Now lower your hand quickly and say what happens and why.
explorations.answer: The hand feels the book pressing down, and must push up just as hard to hold it still - two balanced forces. Remove the hand and gravity is left unopposed, so the book falls.
explorations.hint: Ask yourself what the book would do if your hand were not there. Whatever that is, some force must be preventing it.
explorations.explanation: More Than One Force at Once: a still object is not a force-free object. It is one where the forces cancel, and removing either one starts the motion at once.

methods.title: Drawing a Force Diagram
methods.example: For any object at rest or moving, draw the forces acting on it as labelled arrows and check whether they balance.
steps: Draw the object as a simple box.
Ask what would happen with no forces at all, and name the force that stops it.
Draw an arrow on the object for each force, pointing the way that force acts.
Label every arrow with the name of the force.
If you know the sizes, draw the arrows in proportion - a bigger force gets a longer arrow.
Check: equal arrows in opposite directions mean the motion is not changing.

methods.title: Comparing Two Magnets Fairly
methods.example: To decide which of two magnets is stronger, using a measurement rather than an impression.
steps: Put one paper clip at the zero mark of a flat ruler.
Slide the first magnet slowly along the ruler until the clip first moves, and read the distance.
Repeat twice more and take the average of the three readings.
Do exactly the same with the second magnet, using the SAME clip and the same ruler.
Compare the averages: the magnet that acts from further away is the stronger.
Say how much your three readings differed, so a reader knows how much to trust the comparison.

methods.title: Measuring a Force in Newtons
methods.example: To find the size of a pull using a forcemeter.
steps: Check the forcemeter reads zero before anything is hung on it.
Hang the object from the hook and let it come to rest.
Read the scale with your eye level with the pointer, not from above.
Record the reading in newtons, with the unit written down.
Repeat and average if the pointer is difficult to read steadily.

workedExamples.title: Naming the forces on a kicked ball
workedExamples.prompt: A football has just been kicked and is flying through the air. Name the forces acting on it now.
workedExamples.solution: Two. Gravity pulls it down towards the centre of the Earth. Air resistance pushes back against its movement, slowing it. The kick itself is NOT a force acting on the ball any more - that applied force ended the instant the boot lost contact.

workedExamples.title: Why a parked car does not roll downhill
workedExamples.prompt: A car is parked on a slope with its brakes on and does not move. What forces are acting, and what does that tell you?
workedExamples.solution: Gravity pulls it down the slope. Friction between the tyres and the road pushes up the slope by exactly as much, so the two cancel and the car stays put. The car is still because the forces balance, not because there are none. Release the brake and the friction drops, the forces no longer balance, and it rolls.

workedExamples.title: Is this object a magnet, or just magnetic?
workedExamples.prompt: A steel bar attracts a paper clip. How do you find out whether the bar is a magnet or simply a magnetic material?
workedExamples.solution: Bring a known magnet towards it and turn the known magnet round. If the bar is pushed away with one end of the magnet, the bar is itself a magnet - only two magnets repel. If it is pulled in whichever way round the magnet is held, it is a magnetic material and not a magnet. Attraction alone cannot tell you, because a magnet attracts both.

workedExamples.title: Reading a force diagram
workedExamples.prompt: A diagram of a falling stone shows a 6 N arrow down labelled gravity and a 2 N arrow up labelled air resistance. What is happening, and what happens next?
workedExamples.solution: The arrows do not balance: 6 N down against 2 N up leaves 4 N downward, so the stone is speeding up. As it goes faster the air resistance grows, so the up arrow lengthens. When it reaches 6 N the two balance and the stone stops speeding up, falling instead at a steady speed.

practice.hint: The definition is only four words long.

practice.prompt: What unit is a force measured in?
practice.hint: It is named after a scientist and is written with one capital letter.

practice.prompt: Name the force that pulls everything towards the centre of the Earth.
practice.hint: It is the one force in this unit that needs no contact at all.

practice.prompt: A book rests on a table. Name the two forces acting on it and say why it does not move.
practice.answer: Gravity pulls it down and the normal force from the table pushes it up. They are equal and opposite, so they cancel and the motion does not change.
practice.hint: Ask what the book would do if the table were not there.

practice.prompt: Give one difference between a magnet and a magnetic material.
practice.answer: A magnet attracts magnetic materials; a magnetic material is only attracted BY a magnet and does not attract anything itself.
practice.hint: Try holding two steel nails together and see what happens.

practice.prompt: Name three materials a magnet will NOT attract.
practice.answer: Any three of: aluminium, copper, brass, gold, silver, plastic, wood, glass, paper.
practice.hint: At least one of your three should be a metal, to show that being a metal is not enough.

practice.prompt: Two north poles are brought together. What happens, and what is the rule?
practice.answer: They push apart. Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.
practice.hint: Two of the same always do the same thing.

practice.prompt: Why is repulsion a better test of a magnet than attraction?
practice.answer: A magnet attracts magnetic materials AND the opposite pole of another magnet, so attraction cannot tell the two apart. Only another magnet will push back, so repulsion proves it is a magnet.
practice.hint: Think about what a plain steel nail does when you offer it a magnet, either way round.

practice.prompt: A canoe drifts across a lake at a steady speed. Are the forces on it balanced or unbalanced?
practice.answer: Balanced. Balanced forces mean the motion is not CHANGING, which includes moving at a steady speed as well as standing still.

practice.prompt: Describe a fair way to find out which of two magnets is stronger.
practice.answer: Use the same paper clip and the same ruler for both. Slide each magnet slowly towards the clip and record the distance at which the clip first moves, repeating three times and averaging. The magnet acting from further away is stronger.
practice.hint: Only the magnet may change between the two tests.

activities.title: The magnetic treasure hunt
activities.materials: One magnet, and twenty small objects from around the house of as many different materials as you can find.
steps: Sort the twenty objects into two piles: those you predict the magnet will pick up, and those you predict it will not.
Test each object and move any that surprised you into a third pile.
Look at the third pile and work out what the surprises had in common.
Write one sentence saying what all the attracted objects turned out to be made of.

activities.title: Magnet through the barrier
activities.materials: Two magnets, a paper clip, a sheet of paper, a plastic ruler, a thin book, a steel tin lid.
steps: Put the paper clip on a table and see how close the magnet must come to move it.
Now put a sheet of paper between them and test again. Then the ruler. Then the book.
Record which barriers made no difference and which weakened the pull.
Try the steel lid last, and explain why it behaves differently from all the others.

activities.title: Force arrows around the house
activities.materials: Paper, a pencil, and four everyday situations you can watch.
steps: Choose four things: something resting, something falling, something being pulled, and something floating.
Draw each one as a simple box.
Add and label an arrow for every force you can name on it.
For each drawing, write whether the forces balance, and say how you can tell from the arrows alone.

rules.text: A force is a push or a pull, measured in newtons (N).
Balanced forces mean the motion is not changing - which includes standing still AND moving at a steady speed.
Like poles repel, unlike poles attract.
Only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic. Being a metal is not enough.

terms: A push or a pull, measured in newtons (N).
The unit of force, written N, measured with a forcemeter.
The force pulling everything towards the centre of the Earth, without touching it.
The force between two surfaces sliding past each other, always opposing the sliding.
Friction with the air, which grows the faster you move.
The upward push a liquid gives to anything placed in it.
The push a surface gives back to whatever rests on it.
Forces that cancel, so the motion does not change.
A drawing of an object with a labelled arrow for each force acting on it.
An object that attracts magnetic materials towards it.
A material a magnet attracts: iron, steel, nickel or cobalt.
One of the two ends of a magnet, north or south, which behave differently.
commonMistakes: Only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are. A magnet ignores aluminium, copper, gold and brass, which is exactly how steel cans are sorted from aluminium ones.
A still object has no forces on it.
It usually has at least two that cancel. A book on a table is pulled down by gravity and pushed up by the table by exactly as much.
Anything that a magnet sticks to is a magnet.
It is a magnetic MATERIAL. Two steel nails will not attract each other; only a magnet attracts, and only another magnet will repel.
The kick is still pushing the ball through the air.
The applied force ended the moment the boot lost contact. Only gravity and air resistance act on it after that.

connections.text: A magnet on the fridge door holds a note up because the door is steel. Try it on an aluminium window frame and it drops.
Anyone weighing produce on a hanging spring balance is measuring a force in newtons, then converting it to a mass in kilograms.
Drawing a force diagram turns an invisible push into something you can look at and check.
A steel can and an aluminium can look alike and are separated by a magnet in seconds.

fluency.answer: Any three of: aluminium, copper, brass, gold, silver, plastic, wood, glass, paper.
fluency.hint: At least one of your three should be a metal, to show that being a metal is not enough.
fluency.errorFeedback: Any three of: aluminium, copper, brass, gold, silver, plastic, wood, glass, paper.

fluency.prompt: Two north poles are brought together. What happens, and what is the rule?
fluency.answer: They push apart. Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.
fluency.hint: Two of the same always do the same thing.
fluency.errorFeedback: They push apart. Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.

fluency.prompt: Why is repulsion a better test of a magnet than attraction?
fluency.answer: A magnet attracts magnetic materials AND the opposite pole of another magnet, so attraction cannot tell the two apart. Only another magnet will push back, so repulsion proves it is a magnet.
fluency.hint: Think about what a plain steel nail does when you offer it a magnet, either way round.
fluency.errorFeedback: A magnet attracts magnetic materials AND the opposite pole of another magnet, so attraction cannot tell the two apart. Only another magnet will push back, so repulsion proves it is a magnet.

fluency.prompt: A canoe drifts across a lake at a steady speed. Are the forces on it balanced or unbalanced?
fluency.answer: Balanced. Balanced forces mean the motion is not CHANGING, which includes moving at a steady speed as well as standing still.
fluency.errorFeedback: Balanced. Balanced forces mean the motion is not CHANGING, which includes moving at a steady speed as well as standing still.

fluency.prompt: Describe a fair way to find out which of two magnets is stronger.
fluency.answer: Use the same paper clip and the same ruler for both. Slide each magnet slowly towards the clip and record the distance at which the clip first moves, repeating three times and averaging. The magnet acting from further away is stronger.
fluency.hint: Only the magnet may change between the two tests.
fluency.errorFeedback: Use the same paper clip and the same ruler for both. Slide each magnet slowly towards the clip and record the distance at which the clip first moves, repeating three times and averaging. The magnet acting from further away is stronger.

realProblems.context: A loaded handcart is being pushed along a rough track and keeps slowing down whenever the pusher stops.
realProblems.prompt: Name the force that slows it, and give one thing that would make it easier to push.
realProblems.answer: Friction between the wheels and the track slows it. Better-inflated or smoother wheels, or a smoother track, would reduce the friction and make it easier.
realProblems.hint: The force that opposes sliding is the one that grows on a rough surface.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Friction is the force, and reducing it - smoother wheels or a smoother surface - is what makes the cart easier to push.

realProblems.context: A workshop floor is covered in a mixture of steel screws, aluminium rivets and plastic caps that all need separating.
realProblems.prompt: How would you separate them quickly, and which pile would still be mixed afterwards?
realProblems.answer: Sweep a magnet over the floor to lift out the steel screws. The aluminium rivets and plastic caps are both non-magnetic, so that pile would still be mixed and would have to be sorted another way.
realProblems.hint: A magnet answers one question only: is there iron, steel, nickel or cobalt in it?
realProblems.errorFeedback: A magnet takes out the steel screws in one pass, and leaves aluminium and plastic still mixed together.

realProblems.context: A shop sells two magnets at different prices and claims the dearer one is 'twice as strong'.
realProblems.prompt: Design a test that would check the claim, and say what result would support it.
realProblems.answer: Use the same paper clip and ruler for both, slide each magnet slowly in and record the distance at which the clip first moves, repeating three times and averaging. Keep everything except the magnet the same. A reading roughly twice as far for the dearer magnet would support the claim; a small difference would not.
realProblems.hint: A fair test changes only the magnet, and needs repeats before the difference can be trusted.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Same clip, same ruler, three repeats each, and compare the averaged distances - that is the only way the claim can be checked.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A mango hangs still on a branch. Explain why it does not fall, using the idea of balanced forces.
keyIdeas: Balanced, so the motion does not change
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Gravity pulls the mango down, and the stalk holds it up with an equal and opposite pull. The two forces cancel, so the motion does not change and the mango stays where it is. When the stalk weakens and can no longer match gravity, the forces stop balancing and the mango falls.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A friend says a magnet will pick up any metal. Explain what is wrong, and describe a test that would show it.
keyIdeas: Only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic
Aluminium and copper are metals and are not attracted
Test several metals, not several objects
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: It is wrong because only a few metals are magnetic - iron, steel, nickel and cobalt - and most are not. I would test a steel nail, an aluminium can and a copper wire with the same magnet. The nail is attracted and the other two are not, although all three are metals. That one test settles it.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why is a force diagram more useful than a sentence listing the forces?
keyIdeas: Balance becomes something you can see
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A sentence has to say which way each force points and how big it is, and a reader has to hold all of that in their head. A diagram shows direction by where the arrow points and size by how long it is, so whether the forces balance is something you can see at a glance instead of working out. It is also harder to forget a force when you are drawing the object.
